chapter: Growing up with music in Austin
title: Trumpet versus tuba embouchure
summary: Discussion of why Ramey could not play trumpet and how tuba embouchure differs; Dance mentions John Faddis.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Well, did you say you went on to tuba?

Yeah, after I left trumpet, and I think I had the tuba blocks at the same time I had the trumpet. And then I went to the baritone horn. And then I found that the baritone horn was too much in between. Because I wanted to either learn to play melody or play the bass -- I mean, you know, play the accompaniment. So then I got a tuba. I got an E flat (PHONETIC).
Well, now, when you say you couldn't get the trumpet right, on an instrument like that, the bigger mouthpiece --
I had no trouble with it, you see.
Just a sort of sloppy sort of --
Didn't have that tightness. You don't have to have that tightness, do you?

No, well, I didn't. That comes; it has to be developed. But I didn't have the patience. You know, you have to -- if I had stayed with the trumpet, then I would have been able to play more than just that short octave thing, you know.
But when you played tuba, or whatever, what does that require in the way of sort of embouchure? It doesn't require the same --
Well, you've got more support, because that mouthpiece presses out further, you know. Naturally you don't -- probably don't squeeze your lips as tightly to make a note with the tuba as you do with --
You wouldn't require the sort of muscular development in the same way, would you?

No, because this is -- the trumpet is usually right on the tip of the center of your lip. And that means the muscles have to develop on either side to keep the air from going out, and that was my trouble. When I got to blow a trumpet, air was coming out on both corners of my lips.
Ever since then I noticed -- I saw a film with John Faddis, you know, Dizzy's disciple, and when he was blowing, to the left of his mouth
Well, that's amazing. I don't see how he could do that.

I couldn't figure that. But you could. I mean, each time (inaudible) I don't think that was faked, or anything. No, I'm pretty sure. It's a thing he did out of Colorado last year, when he was playing with Eubie Blake, you know, the oldest and the youngest there. And he played "Memories of You." And you could see his teeth. I don't know how he did that.
I understand. He must have the talent.
